```{r setup}
library(pilotr)
```

## The challenge

A toolkit that spans R and Python faces a subtle obstacle. The two ecosystems use different
default random-number generators (R's Mersenne-Twister with inversion, NumPy's PCG64), so a
direct port produces different data from the same seed. That would undermine the guarantee
that a design authored once can be reproduced anywhere.

## A shared generator

pilotr sets aside the native RNGs and provides a shared generator implemented identically
in both languages. Uniform deviates come from L'Ecuyer's (1988) combined linear congruential
generator, whose arithmetic stays below $2^{53}$ and is therefore exact in IEEE-754 doubles
(R) and Python integers alike. Normal deviates use Wichura's (1988) Algorithm AS 241
inverse-CDF, the algorithm R's `qnorm()` uses. The remaining draws (Cholesky-correlated
random effects, inverse-CDF Poisson and ordinal draws, Marsaglia–Tsang gamma draws for the
Beta family, a Fisher–Yates item sampler for partial crossing) are derived from those two
through a documented, identical consumption order.

As a result, given the same specification and seed, the R and Python implementations produce
identical data sets wherever they share a maths library, as on Linux. Continuous integration
checks every case of the parity harness to the last bit there. IEEE-754 fixes the rounding of
arithmetic but leaves that of `exp()`, `log()` and `pow()` to the library, and on Windows R and
Python do not share one. There, a value that passes through those functions can differ in its
last bits, and every family has such a path. The figures below were measured on Windows 11 with
R 4.6.1 and Python 3.13.

- Normal draws pass through `log()` in AS 241's tail branch, which about 15% of draws take.
  About 1.4e-5 of normal draws differed, by 1 to 3 units in the last place (ulp), so Gaussian
  data can differ too.
- Responses of the lognormal families and the ex-Gaussian differed by 1 ulp.
- An unrounded Beta response differed by up to 35 ulp.
- A discrete outcome can in principle move by a whole category, although none did in 50,000
  rows of each discrete family.

One Beta case can differ on Linux too. From R 4.6.0, R's `^` computes a cube or a fourth power
by repeated multiplication, where Python calls `pow()`. A Beta response whose Gamma shape is
exactly 1/3 or 1/4 can therefore differ in its last bits on any platform. Such a shape needs a
cell whose rows share one linear predictor, as in a Beta design with no random effects, a linear
predictor of 0 and `phi` set to 0.5.

Rounding has removed every continuous difference observed so far, but it guarantees nothing,
since a last-bit difference can straddle a rounding boundary, and `round` is refused for the
discrete families. `build_spec()`, which builds the no-code app's specifications, rounds the
Gaussian, lognormal, shifted lognormal and ex-Gaussian responses to four decimals and leaves a
Beta response unrounded, for the reason `?build_spec` gives. Agreement to the last bit in every
family has one route: run both
languages on a platform where they share a maths library, outside that Beta case. The
specification is the source of truth, and every implementation answers to it. Its section
[Scope of the guarantee](https://github.com/pablobernabeu/pilotr/blob/main/spec/SPEC.md#scope-of-the-guarantee)
gives the measurements in full.

## Determinism in R

On one platform, the same specification and seed always give the same data.

```{r}
spec <- build_spec(list(
  name = "demo", seed = 2024, design_kind = "between", n_subject = 200,
  factor_name = "group", lev1 = "a", lev2 = "b",
  intercept = 100, effect = 5, family = "gaussian",
  resp_name = "score", sigma = 10))

identical(simulate_design(spec), simulate_design(spec))
```

Across operating systems, the same holds on the terms set out above, since R takes `exp()`,
`log()` and `pow()` from the platform's maths library, as Python does.

Changing the seed changes the draws, while the structure and the ground-truth parameters stay
fixed.

```{r}
spec2 <- spec; spec2$seed <- spec$seed + 1L
identical(simulate_design(spec)$score, simulate_design(spec2)$score)
```

## The same design in Python

The Python package reads the same specification and produces the same data. The code below is
not evaluated here. It shows the Python you would run, and its output matches the R data to
the last bit wherever the two share a maths library.

```python
from pilotr import simulate, load_spec

# the same design.json the R package (and the app) use
data = simulate("design.json")
```

The repository includes a parity check that compares the CSV files the R and Python demo
scripts write for six of the shipped example designs, all but the ordinal and Poisson ones, and
reports the maximum absolute difference per design. This is the CSV-level check, read at the
precision a written file carries and with a tolerance of 1e-6. The stricter one is
the harness under `tools/parity/`, which dumps every value at 17 significant digits, accounts
for each differing cell in units in the last place against a recorded allowance, and runs as a
gate in continuous integration. The table below is the readable summary, and that harness is
what the bit-identical claim rests on.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
# Output of python/examples/parity_check.py --csv, precomputed and shipped with
# the package: the comparison needs both a Python and an R installation, so it
# cannot run at vignette build time.
# max_abs_diff is read as text: as a number, kable would round 4.885e-15 to 0
# and the table would claim a stricter result than the check actually produced.
knitr::kable(read.csv("parity-summary.csv",
                      colClasses = c(max_abs_diff = "character")),
             format = "html", table.attr = 'class="table data-output"')
```

The difference is exactly zero for five of the six designs. The sixth, `continuous`
(`reading_time_continuous`), has a rounded response that agrees exactly and continuous
predictors that are not rounded, which R's CSV writer prints to 15 significant digits. Those
predictors differ by about 5e-15. At that precision the residual cannot be told apart from the
writer's own rounding,
and it is what the 1e-6 tolerance of the check is there to absorb. The stricter harness dumps 17
digits and resolves what is really there. On Windows, it finds a handful of cells one unit in
the last place apart, from `exp()`, and no categorical mismatches. On Linux, where it runs in
continuous integration, every cell agrees. The uniform stream is exact by construction, since
every intermediate product stays below $2^{53}$. The harness pins the Gaussian cases to recorded
hashes in `tools/parity/golden.json`, on the observed agreement of AS 241's `log()` across
platforms. The cases are small enough that none has met one of the rare normal draws that
differ. The cases whose values pass through `exp()`, `log()` or `pow()` on the way to the
response are deliberately left unpinned, because those last bits belong to the maths library and
so are not the specification's to fix. The cross-language comparison still gates them on every
run. The parity check can be rerun on any new platform, so a design verified on a laptop can be
confirmed on an HPC node before a large run.

## The analysis layer

Everything above concerns the data the generator produces. `solve_curve()` sits a layer above
it, taking a curve that has already been simulated and fitting a model to it, and it is held to
a different standard on purpose. Its fit calls `exp()` and the normal distribution function at
every iteration, so the two engines cannot be asked to land on the same bits, and a recorded
hash would pin whichever maths library happened to record it. What they are asked for is
agreement far closer than any reading of the result could depend on. The script
`tools/parity/solve_cross.py` puts the same fixed curves through both engines and compares the
solved value, its interval, the fitted coefficients and the text of every refusal. The largest
relative difference measured over those cases is 5.0e-15, against an allowance of 1e-9. On a
solved sample size of 220 subjects that allowance comes to two ten-millionths of a subject.
Every refusal message is identical character for character.

The mixed models of the two `power_mixed()` functions come from `model_formula()` and
`model_data()`, which the Python package ports from this one. The script
`tools/parity/formula_cross.py` gives the Python ports the data R simulated for every shipped
example and parity case. Both must write the same formula character for character and the same
contrast and product columns bit for bit. The fits that follow are another matter. `lme4` and
`statsmodels` are different programs, this package estimates the random-effect correlations that
the Python one leaves out, and the two test with different statistics. The Python power guide sets
out where their results diverge.

`power_report()` writes a sample-size justification from the counts of a result, the
significant replicates and the replicates behind each rate. It computes each Monte Carlo error
with the functions that compute them in both packages, which return the same doubles for the same
counts, and formats them in the same way. The script `tools/parity/report_cross.py` renders a set
of stored records in both engines and requires the same text, byte for byte.

## Why this matters

Because the specification is the source of truth and the generator is shared, a design can be
authored once (in the app, in R or in Python) and reproduced everywhere. It can be preregistered
as a small JSON file that anyone can run, scaled from a laptop to a cluster and handed between
collaborators who work in different languages, with data that agree to the last bit wherever
the machines share a maths library.

This property turns an informal request to simulate some data into a reproducible, shareable
methodological artefact.
